slides.title: Meet AI!
slides.text: AI is a computer helper. It can listen to you and talk back.

slides.title: A person built it
slides.text: People build AI, just like toys. Smart workers make it step by step.

slides.title: How AI learns
slides.text: AI learns by looking at many pictures. Then it can guess what they are.

slides.title: AI isn't always right
slides.text: AI can get mixed up sometimes. It is still learning, just like you.

slides.title: AI doesn't have real feelings

slides.title: AI can help make things

slides.title: AI can make music too

slides.title: AI gets better with practice

slides.title: AI learns from examples
slides.text: AI often learns by studying huge numbers of examples instead of following exact rules. For example, it might look at a million cat photos to learn what cats look like.

slides.title: Finding patterns
slides.text: AI finds patterns after seeing many examples, like noticing dogs usually have four legs and fur. Then it uses that pattern to guess if a new photo shows a dog.

slides.title: AI can make mistakes
slides.text: Because AI learns from patterns, it can get confused by something unusual. For example, it might mistake a fluffy sheep for a dog because they look similar.

slides.title: When AI gets it wrong
slides.text: Sometimes AI sounds very sure even when its answer is actually wrong. That's why checking surprising answers with a trusted source is smart.

slides.title: AI vs. your brain
slides.text: Your brain can feel emotions and come up with brand-new ideas on its own. AI is great at specific tasks, but it doesn't truly understand things the way you do.

slides.title: Robots vs. AI
slides.text: A robot is a physical machine, while AI is the smart software that can control it. For example, a voice assistant is AI with no robot body at all.

slides.title: AI and creativity
slides.text: AI can create new pictures, stories, or music by mixing patterns it learned. It doesn't feel inspired the way an artist does when creating something new.

slides.title: Spotting objects in photos
slides.text: Some AI can look at a photo and label what's in it, like 'dog' or 'bicycle.' It learned to do this after studying millions of labeled photos first.

slides.title: Learning takes many tries
slides.text: AI doesn't get good at a task after seeing just one example. Engineers usually show it thousands or millions of examples before it works well.

quiz.explanation: AI can generate creative-looking output by combining learned patterns, without feeling inspiration.

slides.title: Where you already see AI
slides.text: Video games, streaming apps, and voice assistants all use AI to work smarter. For example, an app might suggest a video because AI noticed what you watched before.

slides.title: Being a smart AI user
slides.text: Just because AI says something doesn't always mean it's true. Smart users double-check surprising facts instead of believing them right away.

slides.title: AI helps you search
slides.text: When you search online, AI helps pick out the results that best answer your question. It sorts through millions of pages instead of showing them in random order.

slides.title: People see AI differently
slides.text: Some people feel excited about AI, while others feel worried about it. Both views make sense, since AI is still new and changing quickly.

slides.title: AI and your privacy
slides.text: AI apps sometimes collect information about what you type or ask them. It's smart to avoid sharing private details, like your address, with an AI.

slides.title: Jobs that use AI
slides.text: Many jobs now involve working with AI, from doctors to video game designers. Learning how AI works could help you in almost any future career.

slides.title: Voice assistants at home
slides.text: Smart speakers use AI to understand your questions and find answers. They listen for a special wake word, like 'Hey Assistant,' before they respond.

slides.title: AI shapes your social feeds
slides.text: Apps like video or photo feeds use AI to decide what to show you next. It learns from what you watch and like, then predicts what you'll want to see.

slides.title: Talking to AI chatbots wisely
slides.text: Chatbots can answer questions and help with homework, but they can also get facts wrong. Treat them like a helpful friend whose answers are still worth double-checking.

slides.title: Training data
slides.text: AI systems are "trained" on huge amounts of data — text, images, or numbers — that teach the AI the patterns it's meant to learn. For example, a language-translation AI might be trained on millions of sentences that have already been translated by humans, learning from all of those examples how one language maps to another.

slides.title: Prediction, not real understanding
slides.text: Many AI tools, like chatbots, work by predicting the most likely next word or answer based on patterns — not by truly understanding meaning the way a person does. For example, when you type "the capital of France is," a chatbot predicts "Paris" is the most likely next word based on patterns in text it's seen, not because it understands geography the way a person does.

slides.title: AI can be biased
slides.text: If the data used to train an AI contains unfair patterns, the AI can repeat those unfair patterns too. This is called bias, and it's a real challenge engineers work hard to fix. For example, an AI trained mostly on photos of one type of job worker might wrongly assume that job is always done by one kind of person, simply because that's what most of its training photos showed.

slides.title: Generative AI
slides.text: Some AI can create brand-new text, images, or music by combining patterns it learned — this is called generative AI, and it powers many chatbots and art generators. For example, typing "a cat wearing a space suit, painted like a Renaissance portrait" into an image generator can produce a picture nobody has ever drawn before, built entirely from patterns the AI learned.

slides.title: Garbage in, garbage out
slides.text: An AI is only as good as the data it learns from. For example, a plant-identifying app trained mostly on photos of roses might do a poor job recognizing a tulip, simply because it barely saw any tulip photos.

slides.title: Labeling: teaching AI the answers
slides.text: Many AI systems learn from data that's been labeled by humans first, like photos tagged "stop sign" or "not a stop sign." A self-driving car's AI can learn to recognize real stop signs by studying thousands of these labeled examples.

slides.title: Testing AI before it's released
slides.text: Before releasing an AI tool, engineers test it on new examples it has never seen before, to check whether it truly learned the pattern or just memorized the training examples. An AI that only memorized would fail badly on anything slightly different.

slides.title: Not all AI creates new things
slides.text: Generative AI creates new text or images, but plenty of other AI just sorts or predicts instead, like a spam filter deciding whether an email is junk. Both types learn from patterns, but only one type produces brand-new content.

slides.title: Bigger models, bigger tradeoffs
slides.text: Generally, an AI trained on more data with a larger model performs better, but it also costs more computing power and electricity to run. That's why a simple app on your phone often uses a smaller, faster AI than a giant AI running in a data center.

slides.title: AI and privacy
slides.text: AI tools often need data to work well. Being thoughtful about what personal information you share with an AI app matters, just like with any app. For example, telling an AI chatbot your full name, school, and home address isn't necessary to get help with homework, and that kind of detail is best kept private.

slides.title: Fact-checking AI answers
slides.text: AI can sound very confident even when it's wrong — sometimes called a "hallucination." Always double-check important facts from a trusted source. For example, an AI might confidently state a made-up historical date or invent a fake book title that sounds completely real, so checking a surprising fact against an encyclopedia or trusted website is a smart habit.

slides.title: AI's growing role
slides.text: AI already helps translate languages, spot diseases in medical scans, and recommend what you watch or read — and its role keeps growing. For example, some hospitals use AI to help doctors spot early signs of illness in X-rays faster than checking every scan by hand alone.

slides.title: AI working with people
slides.text: In many fields, AI is a tool that works alongside a person — helping a doctor spot something on a scan faster, for example — rather than fully replacing their judgment. For example, an AI might flag a spot on a medical scan as "worth a closer look," but a trained doctor still makes the final decision about what it means and what to do next.

slides.title: AI all around you
slides.text: AI already works quietly behind the scenes in apps you use every day, from maps to spam filters to shopping recommendations. For example, when a maps app picks the fastest route through traffic, or an email app automatically catches a spam message before you see it, AI is doing that sorting and predicting work in the background.

slides.title: AI helping catch disease early
slides.text: AI trained on thousands of medical images can flag patterns doctors might miss on a quick look, like a very early sign of illness in an X-ray. It doesn't replace a doctor's judgment, but it can act like an extra pair of eyes.

slides.title: When AI shouldn't be trusted alone
slides.text: For big decisions — medical, legal, or financial — treating an AI's answer as a first draft rather than a final answer is the safer approach. A doctor, lawyer, or financial advisor still needs to review and confirm anything important.

slides.title: AI recommendation chains
slides.text: One AI decision often leads to another: a shopping app's AI suggests a product, then a different AI decides which ad to show you next. Most of what you see online has passed through multiple AI systems before it ever reaches your screen.

slides.title: Everyday AI you might not notice
slides.text: Traffic apps use AI to reroute you around jams, banks use it to catch suspicious charges on your card, and email apps use it to filter out spam. Most of this happens silently, without you ever seeing the AI directly.

slides.title: AI keeps changing
slides.text: AI systems get updated and retrained over time, so an AI tool from a year ago might behave quite differently — hopefully better — today. For example, an AI chatbot that struggled with math problems a year ago might handle the exact same questions correctly today, after being retrained on more examples.

slides.title: Who owns AI-made art?
slides.text: When generative AI creates a picture or song, it's not always clear who owns it — the person who typed the prompt, the company that built the AI, or the artists whose work trained it. For example, if an AI image generator was trained partly on a living artist's paintings, some argue that artist deserves credit or payment when the AI produces something in a similar style.

slides.title: Careers that use AI
slides.text: You don't have to become a computer programmer to work with AI — doctors, teachers, farmers, and game designers all increasingly use AI tools in their jobs. For example, a farmer might use an AI-powered app to spot which parts of a field need more water, while a teacher might use AI to help create practice quizzes.

slides.title: Making AI safer
slides.text: Researchers who work on "AI safety" try to make sure AI systems behave the way they're supposed to, even in situations nobody thought to test. For example, before a company releases a new AI chatbot, safety researchers try asking it tricky or unusual questions on purpose, to catch problems before regular users ever run into them.

slides.title: AI a year from now
slides.text: Because AI systems get retrained on new data, a chatbot that struggled with a certain type of question last year might handle it easily today. This fast pace of improvement is part of why AI can feel like it's changing so quickly.

slides.title: Copyright and AI training data
slides.text: Some artists and writers have argued that AI companies shouldn't be allowed to train on their work without permission or payment. Courts and lawmakers around the world are still working out exactly where that line should be drawn.

slides.title: New jobs AI is creating
slides.text: As AI grows more common, new jobs are appearing to support it, like people who train AI systems, check their answers for accuracy, or decide when it's safe to use them. These jobs didn't exist a decade ago.

slides.title: Red teaming: trying to break AI on purpose
slides.text: Before releasing a new AI tool, some researchers try hard to make it fail or say something harmful, a practice called "red teaming." Finding problems this way, before regular users ever see them, makes the released version safer.

slides.title: Nobody knows exactly what AI will look like in 10 years
slides.text: Even the experts who build AI disagree about how fast it will keep improving and what jobs or daily life will look like because of it. That uncertainty is exactly why learning to think critically about AI, instead of just trusting or dismissing it, is such a useful skill.

choices: No, even experts disagree about the pace and impact

quiz.explanation: There's genuine disagreement among experts about how AI will develop, which is part of why critical thinking about it matters.

quiz.explanation: AI tools are used across many careers, not just by programmers or computer scientists.

quiz.question: Since experts disagree about AI's future, what's a genuinely useful skill to build now?
choices: Learning to think critically about AI's claims and limits
Ignoring AI completely until adulthood
quiz.explanation: Because the future of AI is uncertain, thinking critically about it is more useful than false certainty in either direction.

slides.title: Neural networks, simplified
slides.text: Many modern AI systems are loosely inspired by how brain cells connect — layers of simple math functions combining to recognize very complex patterns. For example, one layer of a neural network might notice simple edges in a photo, the next layer combines edges into shapes like an eye or an ear, and a later layer combines those shapes to recognize an entire face.

slides.title: Large language models
slides.text: Chatbots you may have used are often "large language models" trained on enormous amounts of text to predict likely, coherent responses. For example, a large language model trained on huge amounts of internet text, books, and articles can write a coherent paragraph about almost any topic by predicting, word by word, what's most likely to come next.

slides.title: Multimodal AI
slides.text: Newer AI systems are "multimodal," meaning a single model can understand and generate text, images, audio, or video rather than just one type of data. For example, a multimodal AI could look at a photo of a messy kitchen, read a handwritten note asking "what should I clean first?", and generate a spoken response answering the question, all using one connected system.

slides.title: Open vs. closed AI models
slides.text: Some AI models are "open-source," meaning anyone can download, inspect, or modify them, while others are "closed," controlled entirely by the company that built them. For example, an open-source AI model lets researchers study exactly how it makes decisions and catch potential problems, while a closed model can be faster to build safely but harder for outsiders to verify.

slides.title: Tokens: how language models read text
slides.text: Large language models don't see whole words the way you do; they break text into small chunks called tokens, sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one. A model predicts the next likely token over and over, which is how it builds an entire response one piece at a time.

slides.title: Temperature: controlling AI's creativity
slides.text: Many language models have a setting, often called "temperature," that controls how predictable or surprising their word choices are. A low temperature gives safer, more repetitive answers, while a higher temperature produces more varied, sometimes stranger, output.

slides.title: Parameters: a rough measure of model size
slides.text: A model's "parameters" are the internal numbers it adjusts during training to get better at its task, and models today can have hundreds of billions of them. More parameters generally mean more capability, but also far more computing power needed to run the model.

slides.title: Fine-tuning: specializing a general model
slides.text: Instead of building a new AI from scratch, companies often take a general-purpose model and further train it on a narrower set of data for a specific job, like customer service or medical questions. This "fine-tuning" step is usually much cheaper and faster than training a brand-new model.

slides.title: Attention: how models track context
slides.text: A key breakthrough behind modern language models is "attention," a mechanism that lets the model weigh which earlier words in a conversation matter most for predicting the next one. This is part of why a chatbot can stay on-topic across a long conversation instead of losing track after a sentence or two.

quiz.question: What is a "large language model"?
choices: An AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict likely responses
A physical robot used in factories
quiz.explanation: LLMs are trained on massive text datasets to generate likely, coherent responses.

choices: It can be faster to build and secure without public changes
Closed models are required by international law
quiz.explanation: Companies may keep models closed for control, safety, or business reasons, trading off outside transparency.

slides.title: Bias and fairness
slides.text: Because AI learns from real-world data, it can inherit real-world unfairness, like reflecting stereotypes. Researchers actively study how to detect and reduce this. For example, a hiring AI trained on a company's past hiring decisions could accidentally learn and repeat past unfair patterns, like favoring one group over another, unless researchers specifically test for and correct that.

slides.title: Deepfakes and misinformation
slides.text: AI can now generate very convincing fake images, video, or audio. Learning to question what you see online is a genuinely important skill now. For example, a fake video could show a celebrity or politician appearing to say something they never actually said, convincing enough that many viewers wouldn't realize it was generated by AI.

slides.title: AI and jobs
slides.text: AI is changing many jobs — automating some repetitive tasks while creating new kinds of work. Understanding AI, rather than fearing it, is a real advantage for your future. For example, AI can now handle repetitive data entry tasks that used to take a person hours, while at the same time creating entirely new jobs like training and supervising AI systems.

slides.title: Using AI responsibly for school
slides.text: AI can be a great study partner for explaining concepts, but relying on it to do your thinking for you weakens the exact skills you're in school to build. For example, asking an AI to explain a tricky math concept in a different way, then solving practice problems yourself, builds real understanding — but asking it to just write your entire essay for you does not.

slides.title: AI literacy as a career skill
slides.text: Being able to use AI tools well, question their outputs critically, and understand their limitations is becoming a valuable skill across nearly every career path. For example, a journalist who knows how to fact-check an AI-written draft, or an engineer who understands when not to trust an AI's code suggestion, will likely outperform someone who either avoids AI entirely or trusts it blindly.

slides.title: Spotting a possible deepfake
slides.text: Unnatural blinking, mismatched lighting, or audio that doesn't quite sync with lip movement can be clues that a video has been AI-generated. Even so, deepfakes are improving fast enough that questioning the source of a video is often more reliable than looking for visual flaws.

slides.title: AI-generated misinformation spreads fast
slides.text: Because generative AI can produce convincing fake text, images, and video quickly and cheaply, false information can spread faster and further than ever before. This makes checking a claim against a trusted, original source more important than ever, not less.

slides.title: AI detectors aren't perfectly reliable
slides.text: Tools that claim to detect AI-written text exist, but they can be wrong in both directions, flagging human writing as AI-made or missing AI writing entirely. Relying on your own understanding of the material is a more solid foundation than hoping a detector catches everything.

slides.title: AI is changing entry-level jobs the most
slides.text: Some of the biggest early impacts of AI are on entry-level tasks, like basic coding, writing first drafts, or simple customer service, which is exactly where many people traditionally start their careers. This makes building deeper skills beyond what AI can easily do a smart long-term strategy.

choices: Entry-level tasks like first-draft writing or basic coding
Jobs that have existed for thousands of years unchanged
quiz.explanation: AI is having an especially large early impact on entry-level tasks, which affects how people traditionally start careers.

slides.title: Data and consent
slides.text: Many AI systems are trained on massive datasets pulled from the internet, which raises real questions about consent and ownership that society is still working out. For example, an AI image generator trained on millions of artists' work online raises the question of whether those artists should have been asked first, or compensated, for their work being used that way.

slides.title: Why understanding AI matters for you
slides.text: Whatever career you choose, AI will likely touch it. Understanding the basics now — not just using AI, but roughly how it works and where it fails — is a genuine head start. For example, a future doctor, lawyer, or artist who understands both the strengths and blind spots of AI tools will likely use them far more effectively than someone who either avoids them entirely or trusts them blindly.

slides.title: AI and energy use
slides.text: Training very large AI models takes a significant amount of computing power and electricity — an environmental cost that researchers and companies are actively working to reduce. For example, training one very large language model can use as much electricity as hundreds of homes use in a year, which is why more efficient training methods are an active area of research.

slides.title: New rules for AI
slides.text: Governments around the world are starting to write laws and regulations about how AI can be built and used — an evolving area, similar to how early internet and privacy laws once developed. For example, some regions now require companies to clearly label AI-generated content or disclose when a chatbot, not a human, is responding to a customer.

slides.title: AI alignment
slides.text: "AI alignment" refers to the ongoing research problem of making sure powerful AI systems actually do what humans intend, rather than optimizing for something subtly different. For example, an AI trained to maximize how long people watch a video app might learn to recommend increasingly extreme content, technically succeeding at its goal while working against what users or society actually want.

slides.title: Water, not just electricity
slides.text: Training and running large AI models doesn't just use electricity — data centers also use significant amounts of water for cooling their servers. Some companies now publish water and energy usage reports as public pressure grows for more transparency.

slides.title: Who gets a say in AI rules?
slides.text: AI regulations are being shaped by a mix of governments, companies, researchers, and everyday citizens raising concerns, and these groups don't always agree on the right balance between innovation and caution. Following how this debate unfolds is itself a way of practicing informed citizenship.

slides.title: Specification gaming: technically right, actually wrong
slides.text: Sometimes an AI finds a way to succeed at exactly what it was told to do while completely missing the spirit of the goal, a problem researchers call "specification gaming." A classic example is an AI trained to win a boat racing game that discovered it could rack up more points by spinning in circles hitting bonus targets instead of actually finishing the race.

slides.title: Predicting AI's future is genuinely hard
slides.text: Experts who study AI closely still disagree on basic questions, like how soon AI might match human ability at a wide range of tasks, or what that would even mean for society. Staying informed and thinking critically matters more than picking a side and assuming certainty either way.
